books.section: Topic 8.6 Early Steps in the Civil Rights Movement (1940s and 1950s)
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)
Civil Rights Act of 1957, Pub. L. 85-315, September 9, 1957

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the photograph is a public-domain U.S. Army photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the federal government advanced civil rights from 1941 to 1957.

documents.title: Fair employment in defense work
documents.source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Executive Order 8802, June 25, 1941. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A presidential order issued after A. Philip Randolph threatened a march on Washington over exclusion from defense jobs.
documents.text: The order banned discrimination in defense industries and in the federal government because of race, creed, color, or national origin. It created a Fair Employment Practice Committee to hear complaints and investigate discrimination in war work.

documents.title: The Double V
documents.source: The Pittsburgh Courier, Double V campaign, February 1942. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A leading Black newspaper's campaign, speaking to Black readers during the war and pressing the government for change.
documents.text: The Courier called for a double victory: victory over fascism abroad and victory over racism at home. Black Americans would serve loyally in the war, and in return the nation should live up to its ideals and end discrimination at home.

documents.title: Equality in the armed forces
documents.source: President Harry S. Truman, Executive Order 9981, July 26, 1948. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A presidential order issued after Congress refused to pass the civil rights laws Truman's committee had recommended.
documents.text: The order declared that there should be equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed forces, without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. It said the policy should take effect as rapidly as possible, and it created a committee to study service rules and recommend changes.

documents.title: Separate schools are unequal
documents.source: Chief Justice Earl Warren, Brown v. Board of Education, May 17, 1954. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A unanimous Supreme Court opinion, written by the chief justice, deciding five combined school cases.
documents.text: The Court ruled that separating children in public schools by race was unconstitutional. It found that segregation harmed Black children and that separate educational facilities were inherently unequal, overruling the separate-but-equal rule of Plessy v. Ferguson.

documents.title: Desegregation with all deliberate speed
documents.source: Chief Justice Earl Warren, Brown II, May 31, 1955. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A follow-up Supreme Court ruling, issued a year after Brown, telling lower courts how to carry out desegregation.
documents.text: The Court told school districts to make a prompt and reasonable start toward desegregation and to proceed with all deliberate speed. It gave the lower federal courts the job of judging whether each district was moving fast enough, but it set no date for finishing.

documents.title: Federal troops at Central High
documents.source: Photograph: Operation Arkansas, Little Rock Nine, September 1957. U.S. Army photograph, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A U.S. Army photograph of the federal troops sent to enforce a court order against a governor's defiance.
documents.text: The photograph shows a student of the Little Rock Nine arriving at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, escorted by soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division. Governor Orval Faubus had used the Arkansas National Guard to block the nine Black students, and President Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent about 1,000 paratroopers.

documents.title: A first civil rights law
documents.source: Civil Rights Act of 1957, Pub. L. 85-315, signed September 9, 1957. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: The first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction, passed after Southern opposition in the Senate watered it down.
documents.text: The act was a voting rights law. It created a Civil Rights Commission to investigate discrimination in voting and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department to prosecute interference with the right to vote. It gave the government new tools, but its enforcement was weak.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the federal government advanced civil rights from 1941 to 1957, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of the federal government's advance does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as Jim Crow segregation, World War II and the Double V campaign, or the Cold War pressure on American democracy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as the fair employment order, Executive Order 9981, or the Brown decision.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about how far the federal government advanced civil rights.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as Jackie Robinson's debut in 1947, the Montgomery Bus Boycott, or the NAACP's Sweatt and McLaurin cases of 1950.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement about civil rights with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as the Courier writing to Black readers during the war or the Brown II Court leaving enforcement to lower courts.
rubric.notEarned: Describing what a document says without explaining why its source matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by branch of government, explaining why the courts moved faster than Congress, or weighing federal advances against the limits that left most segregation standing.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The federal government advanced civil rights a long way from 1941 to 1957, moving from a single wartime employment order to a Supreme Court ruling against school segregation, but the advance was uneven and mostly left enforcement to others, so most segregation still stood in 1957.
Context: Jim Crow ruled the South, the armed forces were segregated, and Black Americans were shut out of defense jobs and voting. World War II and the Cold War made that gap hard to defend, at home and abroad.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 3 show the executive branch moving first, with fair employment in 1941 and military desegregation in 1948. Documents 4 and 5 show the courts moving furthest, with Brown ending school segregation and Brown II ordering desegregation with all deliberate speed but no deadline. Document 6 shows the president using troops at Little Rock, and Document 7 shows Congress finally acting with a voting rights law. Document 2 shows the pressure from below that pushed the government.
Outside evidence: Jackie Robinson broke baseball's color line in 1947, the NAACP won Sweatt and McLaurin in 1950, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott held for 381 days before the courts ended bus segregation.
Complexity: The advance looks different by branch. The courts declared the principle, the presidents acted by order and by troops, and Congress moved last and weakest, so the extent of the advance depends on which branch is measured.
